Imagine if your profiles lived on your personal computers, and access to "add friends" and view their profiles was done by some sort of key exchange (but more simplified, IE "permit so and so with this email address to access my profile").

I feel like social media is a great tool for many reasons, but it's also incredibly scary when you start thinking about privacy, doxxing, and what the company that hosts it does with your data. How secure is your data on their servers? Etc.

If I no longer wanted to be a part of this network, I could just simply shut my profile off on my computer at home and call it a day.

No company would simply be able to look up my profile, as you'd need to have explicit permission from the user to have access to their profile.

I realize (as I work in IT) that there are a few gotchas with this kind of idea, but I'm certain it could be done, and even to the simplicity where mom and dad could figure out how to set it up.
Wouldn't it be nice if something like Facebook existed, but was decentralized and the user was in control of who had access to what data?

I wonder if that's what the people behind Diaspora were thinking.

edit: There's also this table comparing most, if not all available decentralized social networks.
Wow, there are a lot more out there than I thought...

How would someone access/comment on your profile when you are offline? Either there would have to be a server with all that data, connected 24/7, or users would have to access profiles from the currently online users. Either way, you are not control of your data.

Lastly, if you want access to other people's profiles while they are offline, you'd have to store that data on your device, which would get enormously large in a hurry.

Hey now, I didn't say I had all the answers!

But seriously. For someone like me that probably has <50 people I ever care to stay in contact with, I doubt that shit would take up much space.

As for offline viewing, perhaps caching, or perhaps home servers become a thing in the near future. I have one. Hardware and other stuff keeps getting cheaper so you never know.

Poking holes in an idea is part of the problem solving process. I like the idea, in theory, as much as you do, but you should think of ways to overcome the downsides of the idea if you want to make it reality. I doubt people will build servers just to house their social media. If you want to make this idea reality you have to make it as easy as Facebook for the user. Data usage is a huge downside of distributed networks and needs to be addressed.
